food.text: The first Greek cookbook was printed on the island of Syros in 1828. Greek cuisine, founded on wheat, olive oil and wine, had been recorded in images and texts since ancient times.

The English word moussaka was borrowed from Greek mousakás and from other Balkan languages, all of which took it from Ottoman Turkish. It is first attested in English in 1862, in a translation of a Turkish cookbook called Melceü't-Tabbâhîn.

The first ouzo distillery was founded in Tyrnavos in 1856 by Nikolaos Katsaros, giving birth to the famous ouzo Tyrnavou. Modern ouzo distillation largely took off at the beginning of the 19th century, following Greek independence.

Until the last decades of the 19th century, raki was made exclusively at home, with no mass industrial production. Colorless spirits such as tsipouro, raki, arak and grappa were distilled from the by-products of wine, getting as much as possible out of the vineyard.
Under Ottoman rule, pork became popular in northern Serbia because pigs were not taxed under Ottoman Islamic law.

One popular explanation for the name "ouzo" is that Thessaly exported fine silkworm cocoons to Marseilles in the 19th century. Crates were stamped "uso Marsiglia", Italian for "to be used in Marseille", and the phrase came to stand for superior quality.

In the Ottoman Empire, until the 19th century, meyhanes (taverns) run by Rûm (Greeks) and Albanians mainly served wine along with meze. This was because of religious restrictions imposed by various sultans.

The oldest modern Serbian cookbook was written in 1855 by the Orthodox monk Jerotej of Krušedol. The first cookbook published in Serbia was The Big Serbian Cookbook, written by Katarina Popović-Midzina in 1877.

Tomatoes had entered Ottoman cooking by the 1690s but are missing from the few surviving 18th-century recipe manuscripts. Mehmet Kamil's influential 1844 manuscript includes recipes for tomato stew, stuffed tomato dolma and tomato pilaf.
Ouzo Plomari, a historic Greek ouzo company on the island of Lesvos, was founded in 1894 by Isidoros Arvanitis, a native of Plomari. Today it exports to more than 40 countries.
Pata's Cookbook, written by Spasenija Pata Marković in 1907, is the best known Serbian cookbook. It remains in publication even today.

The Karelia family established a small tobacco business in Kalamata, Greece, in 1888. Its activities were largely regional for the first few decades, and it later grew into Greece's largest tobacco manufacturer and exporter.

art.text: Because few opportunities for an education in the arts existed in newly independent Greece after centuries of Ottoman rule, artists had to study abroad. Most Greek artists of the 19th century chose Munich, an important international centre for the arts. There they formed the bonds that gave birth to the Greek "Munich School" of painting.

The most important artistic movement of Greek art in the 19th century was academic realism, often called in Greece "the Munich School". It painted the same sort of scenes in the same sort of style as Western European academic painters, and generally did not try to incorporate Byzantine stylistic elements.
art.source_title: Greek academic art of the 19th century
tags: Royal Academy of Fine Arts of Munich

art.text: Modern Greek art was shaped by the particular socioeconomic conditions of Greece, the large Greek diaspora across Europe, and the new Greek social elite. External influences, predominantly from Germany and France, also mattered. Some Greek artists remained in Munich, which was nicknamed "Athens on the Isar".

Serbian art was marked in the mid-19th century by Biedermeier civil works alongside a program of historicism. Serbian painters' education and stays in Vienna and Munich, and trips to Italy, were crucial for Romanticism to penetrate. Romanticism reached its highest achievements in the late 1860s and beginning of the 1870s.

Neoclassical architecture was heavily used for public and private buildings in Greece after independence and throughout the nineteenth century. The architecture of Athens and other cities of the Kingdom of Greece was shaped mostly by architects such as Theophil Hansen, Ernst Ziller and Stamatios Kleanthis. Churches, meanwhile, experienced a Neo-Byzantine revival.

Theodoros Vryzakis (1814-1878) and Dionysios Tsokos (1820-1862) were among the first painters of free Greece. Both drew their subjects from the Greek War of Independence in 1821. They focused on idealised ideas of the revolution and gave little attention to the violent and tragic aspects of war.
art.source_title: Greek academic art of the 19th century

art.text: Nikiphoros Lytras (1832-1904) is considered the pope of Greek painting and the major iconographer of Greek life in the 19th century. Paintings such as The milkman and The awaiting are reference points in Greek art.
art.source_title: Greek academic art of the 19th century

art.text: Georgios Iacovidis (1853-1907) painted mainly portraits and scenes depicting children. He was also the founder and first curator of the National Gallery of Greece in Athens.
art.source_title: Greek academic art of the 19th century

art.text: In 19th-century Serbian culture, the golden age of the nation was equated with the rule of the Nemanjić dynasty. Historicist painters such as Đura Jakšić (1832-1878) and Pavle Simić (1818-1876) idealised events and personalities to awaken national and patriotic feelings. The most productive period of Historicism in Serbian art was 1848 to 1878.

Tower houses were typically made of stone, rose three or four storeys, and were square or rectangular. They served both military purposes (defence, watchtower) and civilian ones (residential), in order to protect the extended family. The practice became very widespread among Christian and Muslim communities during the decline of Ottoman power in the 17th century and flourished until the early 20th century.

Later painters such as Konstantinos Volanakis (1837-1907) and Ioannis Altamouras (1852-1878) were even more dramatic in their depictions. They focused more on the naval battles of the 1821 Revolution.
art.source_title: Greek academic art of the 19th century

art.text: Nikolaos Gysis (1842-1901) worked mainly on ethography. In the maturity of his career he shifted towards the iconography of visions, allegories and symbolisms. Unlike other painters of the school, he stayed at the Academy in Germany rather than returning to teach at the Athens School of Fine Arts.
art.source_title: Greek academic art of the 19th century

art.text: The Heptanese School of painting led Greek post-Byzantine art from the middle of the 17th century until the middle of the 19th century. It was based in the Ionian islands, which were not part of Ottoman Greece. It combined Byzantine traditions with growing Western European influence and made the first significant depiction of secular subjects.

Georgios Roilos (1867-1928) began under the Munich School but went beyond its principles in his mature career. He introduced impressionism into Greek painting. Periclis Pantazis (1849-1884) had also departed from academic realism towards impressionism after the mid-19th century.
art.source_title: Greek academic art of the 19th century

war.text: The Greek War of Independence was fought by Greek revolutionaries against the Ottoman Empire from 1821 to 1829. It led to the formation of modern Greece. Greeks still commemorate the revolution on 25 March as Independence Day.

The First Balkan War lasted from October 1912 to May 1913, as Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece and Montenegro of the Balkan League fought the Ottoman Empire. It was a comprehensive and unmitigated disaster for the Ottomans, who lost 83% of their European territories and 69% of their European population. Many civilians, overwhelmingly Muslim Turks, were either killed or forced to flee their homes, because the disorganized Ottoman army could not evacuate them and left them defenseless against the invading armies. Both sides committed war crimes, and about 890,000 civilians of various nationalities crossed borders in 1912–1914, though the number of civilian casualties is disputed.

Greece's part in the Balkan Wars of 1912–1913 allowed the Greek state to almost double its size. It also brought to prominence Prime Minister Eleftherios Venizelos and the Army's commander-in-chief, Crown Prince Constantine, later King Constantine I.

The secret Filiki Eteria was founded in 1814 by Nikolaos Skoufas, Emmanuil Xanthos and Athanasios Tsakalov to liberate Greece. The insurrection was planned for 25 March 1821, the Feast of the Annunciation, but Ottoman authorities discovered the plans and forced an earlier start.
In 1827 Russia, Britain and France sent naval squadrons to Greece. They destroyed the Ottoman–Egyptian fleet at the Battle of Navarino, which turned the tide in favor of the revolutionaries.

An economic depression and a catastrophic defeat in the Thirty Days' War weakened the Greek state. Poverty was rife in the countryside and islands, and Greece was virtually bankrupt. The Goudi coup in 1909 then brought Eleftherios Venizelos to power and sweeping reforms, culminating in the Hellenic Army's victory in the Balkan Wars. The Ottomans estimated that 15,000 officers and men were killed in the Macedonia campaign alone, bringing their total losses there up to 41,000 soldiers.

In 1912 the core of the Greek fleet was the armoured cruiser Georgios Averof, completed in 1910 and then the fastest and most modern warship in the combatant navies. It was complemented by three rather-antiquated battleships of the Hydra class and eight destroyers built in 1906–1907.

The Army of Thessaly occupied much of Macedonia in the First Balkan War, including the port of Thessaloniki, just hours ahead of a Bulgarian division. This increased tension between the two allies and became one of the causes of the Second Balkan War.
Nenadović's Tower was built by Jakov Nenadović in 1813 in Valjevo. It was first used by rebels during the First Serbian Uprising of the Serbian Revolution. The Ottomans later used it as a prison.

In 1828 the Egyptian army withdrew under pressure from a French expeditionary force, and the Ottoman garrisons in the Peloponnese surrendered. The Ottomans then declared war on Russia, letting the Russian army move into the Balkans. This forced them to accept Greek autonomy in the Treaty of Adrianople, and semi-autonomy for Serbia.

Bulgaria was called the "Prussia of the Balkans" and had the region's strongest army, while the Greek army was held in low esteem after the 1897 debacle. Greece could offer its navy, which alone could stop Ottoman reinforcements arriving from Asia. A treaty of defensive alliance was signed at Sofia on 29 May 1912.

On the night of 30 (17) June 1913, General Savov, acting under direct orders from Tsar Ferdinand I and without consulting the Bulgarian government or declaring war, attacked the Serbian army at the Bregalnica river and then the Greek army in Nigrita. The Serbs resisted the sudden night attack, but most of their soldiers did not even know who they were fighting, because Bulgarian camps lay right next to Serb ones and the Bulgarians were considered allies. The Greek army then counterattacked and, after taking Kilkis, plundered and burnt the mostly Bulgarian town while part of its mostly Bulgarian population was massacred. In reprisal the Bulgarian army destroyed Nigrita, Serres and Doxato and massacred non-combatant Greek inhabitants at Sidirokastro and Doxato.

In 1823 Hussein Bey led a well-organised Turkish-Egyptian force of 12,000 soldiers with artillery and cavalry against Crete. Emmanouil Tombazis gathered 3,000 men in Gergeri to face him, but the Cretans were defeated and lost 300 men at the battle of Amourgelles on 20 August 1823.

literature.text: Between 1830 and 1880, Romanticism was the dominant movement in Greek literature. The first Greek state covered only a small part of the present-day mainland and a few islands, so nationalism was ever-present in the writing of the first decades. Gradually other themes emerged.

Serbian epic poems and folk tales had been almost exclusively an oral tradition, passed on by bards and singers. In the first half of the 19th century, the ethnographer Vuk Karadžić collected many of them and published them in books.

After the establishment of the Kingdom of Greece, intellectual output centered in the Ionian Islands and in Athens. The Heptanese School included Dionysios Solomos, who wrote the national anthem of Greece, and Aristotelis Valaoritis. The Athenian School included Alexandros Rizos Rangavis and Panagiotis Soutsos.
The National Theatre of Greece was founded in 1880. Notable playwrights of the modern Greek theatre include Alexandros Rizos Rangavis and Gregorios Xenopoulos.

Many participants of the Greek War of Independence, including Theodoros Kolokotronis, wrote memoirs. They matter for their literary value as well as for history, because they are written in a lively demotic language. Yannis Makriyannis's memoir, written between 1829 and 1850, is considered a landmark of Greek literature.
Emmanuel Rhoides was a fierce and indefatigable satirist. His best-known book, The Papess Joanne (1866), was inspired by a famous legend. It is considered a classic of Greek literature today.
Demetrios Vikelas, a prolific author and translator, wrote the historical novel Loukis Laras in 1879. It stands out for its naturalistic style and marked the beginning of a new era for Greek prose.

Foreign scholars first gave Europe Albanian folklore in the second half of the 19th century, which began the scholarly study of Albanian oral tradition. The Austrian consul Johann Georg von Hahn recorded folk songs and tales while travelling through Albania and the Balkans. He published them in 1854 as Albanesische Studien.

Iakovos Pitsipios wrote the satire Xouth the Ape in 1849. It is regarded as Greece's first sociological novel. Even though prose fiction was mostly cultivated in Athens, this work was far from the spirit of the Athenian School.

The Ionian islands reunited with Greece in 1864 and continued to be a major intellectual centre. At the same time, several men of letters from unredeemed lands gathered in Athens, which led to the so-called First Athenian School.

The German physician Karl H. Reinhold collected Albanian folklore from Albanian sailors while he was serving as a doctor in the Greek navy. In 1855 he published the material as Noctes Pelasgicae, or Pelasgian Nights.

The Danish Indo-Europeanist Holger Pedersen visited Albania in 1893 to learn the language and gather linguistic material. He recorded thirty-five Albanian folk tales from Albania and Corfu. He published them in 1895 as Albanesische Texte mit Glossar.

In 1881, Elodie Lawton reported that Anta Neshich, a member of the National Assembly of Serbia from Ripanj, amused his listeners in an unusual way. He would recount debates over a monetary reform bill in the style of epic poetry.

science.text: The idea of a Balkan Peninsula was created in 1808 by the German geographer August Zeune. He mistakenly believed the Balkan Mountains were the dominant mountain system of southeastern Europe, stretching from the Adriatic Sea to the Black Sea.

From 1876 onwards, after a Serb and Montenegrin uprising and the Russo-Turkish War of 1877-1878, a large number of maps of the Balkans' ethnic demographics were published. Greeks, Serbs, Bulgarians and Turks used them to justify their territorial claims, especially over Macedonia. The phenomenon has been labelled "map mania".
science.source_title: Ethnographic cartography of the Balkans in the late 19th and early 20th century

science.text: Many Balkan ethnic maps of this era were built to give an impression of uniformity. They showed ethnic groups as blocks of solid colors and ignored population density. Substantial minorities, even up to 49 percent in some cases, were omitted.
science.source_title: Ethnographic cartography of the Balkans in the late 19th and early 20th century

science.text: Not every geographer accepted Zeune's idea. Carl Ritter warned that only the part south of the Balkan Mountains could be considered a peninsula, and suggested renaming it the "Greek peninsula". Hermann Wagner, Theobald Fischer, Marion Newbigin and Albrecht Penck also disagreed with Zeune.
Heinrich Kiepert's 1876 map of the Balkans was particularly influential. It was used at the Congress of Berlin.
science.source_title: Ethnographic cartography of the Balkans in the late 19th and early 20th century

science.text: After the Congress of Berlin in 1878 there was a political need for a new term, and "the Balkans" was gradually revitalized. On many maps, though, the northern border lay in Serbia and Montenegro, and Greece was not included.

The early maps by Ami Boué and Guillaume Lejean were influential and generally favorable to the Bulgarians. But they greatly exaggerated the Albanian presence towards the south, and their reputation suffered as a result.
science.source_title: Ethnographic cartography of the Balkans in the late 19th and early 20th century

science.text: In 1869, the Austrian diplomat Johann Georg von Hahn used the term Südosteuropäische Halbinsel, meaning Southeastern European peninsula, for the same territory. It was an alternative to Zeune's Balkan Peninsula.

Greek efforts produced three pro-Greek maps, by Stanford, Bianconi and Synvet, but they had little impact and no one outside Greece took them seriously. Greek maps counted as Greeks not only Greek-speakers but also Christian Vlachs, Christian Albanians and Exarchist Slavs, an approach international figures rejected.
science.source_title: Ethnographic cartography of the Balkans in the late 19th and early 20th century

politics.text: In 1832 the Treaty of Constantinople formally recognised Greece as an independent state and made it a monarchy. This followed the Greek War of Independence and ended nearly four centuries of Ottoman rule. The new kingdom's main ideological goal became the Megali Idea, which sought to annex lands with predominantly Greek populations.

In 1912 Greece, Bulgaria, Montenegro and Serbia formed the Balkan League and attacked the Ottoman Empire. They stripped it of its European provinces, leaving only Eastern Thrace under Ottoman control. The war set the stage for the July crisis of 1914 and was a prelude to the First World War.

King Otto ruled Greece as an absolute monarch from 1835 until the 3 September 1843 Revolution. That revolution made Greece a constitutional monarchy, creating the office of Prime Minister as head of government, universal male suffrage and a constitution.

A popular insurrection deposed King Otto in 1862, which precipitated the gradual collapse of the early Greek parties, known as the English, French and Russian parties. The Greek National Assembly then elected George I in 1863. His election brought the transfer of the Ionian Islands from British rule in 1864.

Prime Ministers such as Alexandros Koumoundouros and Charilaos Trikoupis shaped the politics and identity of the Greek kingdom, including the annexation of Thessaly in 1881. Later an economic depression and a catastrophic defeat in the Thirty Days' War weakened the Greek state.

The Goudi coup of 1909 brought Eleftherios Venizelos to power and led to sweeping reforms. His reforms included a major revision of the Greek Constitution of 1864, producing the Greek Constitution of 1911, described as a major step forward in Greece's constitutional history.

In 1908 the Young Turks, led by the Committee of Union and Progress, rebelled against Sultan Abd-ul-Hamid II. They removed him from power and restored the empire to a constitutional monarchy. They replaced him with Sultan Mehmed V, described as ineffective.

From the 1860s onwards, Edessa, then called Vodena, was a flashpoint for clashes between Greeks and Bulgarians. The Ottoman census of 1881/1882-1893 counted 14,962 Muslims, 14,208 Greek Patriarchists and 3,943 Bulgarian Exarchists in the district.

Profiting from civil strife in the Ottoman Empire, Austria-Hungary officially annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1908. Within a few years the Ottomans also lost their North African territories and the Dodecanese in the Italo-Turkish War of 1911.

The Petrović-Njegoš family transformed Montenegro into a principality in 1852 and ruled until 1918. Before that, from 1696 until 1852, the metropolitans of Cetinje of the same house ruled Montenegro alongside tribal rulers. Independence of the Principality of Montenegro was received in 1878.

Montenegro followed Bulgaria's precedent in August 1910 by becoming a kingdom. Bulgaria had secured Ottoman recognition of its independence in April 1909 and enjoyed the friendship of Russia. It also looked to annex districts of Ottoman Thrace and Macedonia.

In 1904 Stephanos Dragoumis formed the Macedonian Committee in Athens. It supported the Macedonian Struggle, in which Greece sent military officers to form bands of Macedonians and Greek volunteers against Ottoman and Bulgarian forces. The struggle lasted from 1904 to 1908 and ended with the Young Turk Revolution.

philosophy.text: Theophilos Kairis was an Orthodox priest and philosopher who became a leading intellectual of the Greek Revolution. On 10 May 1821 he declared the War of Independence by raising the Greek flag at the cliffside church of St George on the island of Andros.

Petar II Petrović-Njegoš was both Prince-Bishop of Montenegro and a poet and philosopher, and he is best known for his epic poem Gorski vijenac (The Mountain Wreath), whose author drew on Serb folklore and oral tradition. His reign was also violent. A council of chieftains condemned the Radonjić brothers to death for treason, though Njegoš later commuted the sentence to exile. He gave his word that the Božović brothers would not be harmed, yet they were arrested and executed by firing squad, and he had rebels shot. After he persuaded the Drobnjaci to ambush Smaïl-aga, a warrior cut off the dead man's head with an axe and brought it to him. He also turned an unfinished tower, the Tablja, into a place where the heads of decapitated Turkish warriors were impaled on spears and left exposed to the elements.

In 1803 Adamantios Korais published his Report on the Present State of Civilization in Greece, based on lectures he had given in Paris. It extolled the link between the rise of a new Greek mercantile class and the advance of the Modern Greek Enlightenment.

The pamphlet Hellenic Nomarchy, published in 1806, advocated freedom, social justice and social equality for the Greek people. By 1814 the Filiki Eteria had formed in Odessa, aiming to overthrow Ottoman rule and establish an independent Greek State.

From 1826 Kairis devoted himself to an orphan school on Andros for the orphans of the Greek revolution. Many of the children were orphans of the war, especially of the massacre on the island of Psara. There he introduced subjects including comparative religion, astronomy, ship navigation, agriculture and natural science.

In 1808 Konstantinos Koumas took over the Philological Gymnasium of Smyrna, where he taught philosophy, experimental physics and ethics. He introduced rationalism and experimentation, displacing the ecclesiastical tradition of teaching based on memorization and obedience.

Neophytos Vamvas was the first dean of the philosophical school at the University of Athens. He was considered the teacher of the nation and was one of the most influential figures of modern Greek education.

Adamantios Korais created the Hellenic Library, devoted to new editions of classical texts, starting with Homer in 1805. Many volumes followed, with lengthy prefaces by Korais titled 'Impromptu Reflections' that set out his views on political, educational and linguistic matters.

King Otto offered Kairis the directorship of the University of Athens, but he refused and kept teaching radical Enlightenment ideas. After the Holy Synod convicted him in 1839, he was confined on Skiathos, and he died in 1853, ten days before his judicial hearing.

Neophytos Vamvas translated the Bible into modern Greek, publishing the New Testament in 1833 and the Old Testament in 1850. Ultraconservative circles in the Church of Greece opposed it, and the Holy Synod disapproved of the publication between 1835 and 1836. The Ecumenical Patriarchate in Constantinople issued an encyclical in 1836 condemning any translation of the Bible into vernacular Greek, and publishing the book was forbidden. His version was finally allowed only in 1924.

When the Greek Revolution began, the Turkish authorities confiscated Konstantinos Koumas's property, including his library, and he escaped on an Austrian ship to Trieste. In Vienna he later wrote a History of Human Acts in 12 volumes, his most important intellectual creation.

In 1805 Korais wrote What should we Greeks do in the Present Circumstances?, trying to win his compatriots over to Napoleon and away from their Russian co-religionists. In later years his enthusiasm faded, and he ended by calling the French Emperor the 'tyrant of tyrants.'
tags: What should we Greeks do in the Present Circumstances?

culture.text: Mid-19th century studies found that almost all the men who built walls, felled trees and sawed lumber in the European part of the Ottoman Empire and in the Kingdom of Greece came from Albania's mountainous regions. Albanian carpenter-masons had a strong reputation among Ottoman and European elites for advanced residential housing.

Cappadocian Greeks of the 19th and 20th centuries were renowned for the richness of their folktales and for preserving their ancient Greek tongue. In 1838 the British scholar Robert Ainsworth described them as pleasing and unreserved in manners, with a very high degree of intelligence.

Cinema first appeared in Greece in 1896, but the first actual cine-theatre did not open until 1907. In 1914, the Asty Films Company was founded and began producing long films in Greece. Golfo, a well-known traditional love story, is regarded as the first Greek long movie.

Before the First World War, Edessa was well on its way to becoming a major industrial center in Macedonia. It had four large textile factories, the biggest being the Hemp Factory, which used the abundant waterfalls as a source of energy.

As late as the 20th century, the Cappadocian underground cities were still used as refuges from periodic waves of Ottoman persecution. The Cambridge linguist Dawkins, who researched the area from 1909 to 1911, recorded that in 1909, when news came of the massacres at Adana, a great part of the population at Axo took refuge in these underground chambers. For some nights they did not venture to sleep above ground.

Pontic crypto-Christians such as the Kromlides bore both a Muslim and a Christian name, and many were linked to mining communities with privileges like exemption from military service. The Kromlides declared themselves Christians in 1857, and the Stavriotes did so in 1876 after the Ottoman Constitution was signed. Declarations of religion were often political rather than based solely in faith.
